name: Industrial Training
description: Industrial training connects practical occupational learning with the requirements of production, maintenance, and technological change. In Iran, instructor development provides a documented connection between vocational institutions and industrial skills, although the evidence inspected does not establish nationwide training outcomes.

seo.title: Industrial Training in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iran’s industrial skills training, instructor development, modernization priorities, and the limits of available evidence.

content.heading: Connecting instruction with industrial work
content.content:
Industrial training concerns the practical capabilities needed to perform and improve work in industrial settings. A useful distinction separates teaching an occupation from ensuring that instruction matches the equipment, processes, and responsibilities encountered at work. The United Nations Industrial Development Organization, or UNIDO, frames this challenge internationally around employer partnerships, practical competencies, and training systems that respond to industrial demand. This is a general framework, rather than a measurement of Iran’s performance. [s1](https://www.unido.org/cross-cutting-priorities/skills-development)

For Iran, the Instructor Training Center in Karaj offers a concrete institutional example. Its role is to prepare instructors for the Technical and Vocational Training Organization, commonly abbreviated TVTO, and affiliated institutions. The UNESCO-UNEVOC directory identifies technical specializations including welding, automotive technology, electricity, mechatronics, and computer numerical control, or CNC—the computerized control of machine tools. This range illustrates why industrial training depends on instructors with different occupational expertise. It does not establish how widely each specialization is available to learners across Iran. [s2](https://connect.unevoc.unesco.org/home/Explorez%2Ble%2BR%C3%A9seau%2BUNEVOC/centre=3071)

content.heading: Modernization involves teachers as well as equipment
content.content:
A UNESCO procurement assignment with a May 2025 application deadline documents a modernization project at the Karaj center, supported by the Korea International Cooperation Agency, or KOICA. Its background connects changes in teaching with labor-market relevance, staff capabilities, and support for young people. The assignment required equipment proposals to be checked against technical specifications, market availability, budgets, and departmental priorities. These are documented project requirements; the document does not certify that procurement or installation was completed. [s3](https://iran.un.org/en/download/184181/294666)

The distinction matters when interpreting announcements about training infrastructure. A procurement plan establishes intended investment, while evidence of delivery would require equipment acceptance records, operational workshops, trained instructors, and subsequent teaching activity. None of those outcomes should be inferred solely from a consultant’s terms of reference. [s3](https://iran.un.org/en/download/184181/294666)

content.heading: What would demonstrate industrial relevance?
content.content:
UNIDO’s international approach places green and digital capabilities alongside conventional technical skills. Its examples include manufacturing, renewable energy, and the circular economy, in which resources remain in use through practices such as reuse and recovery. This provides a useful lens for examining industrial curricula, without assuming that all Iranian providers already teach these subjects. [s1](https://www.unido.org/cross-cutting-priorities/skills-development)

The evidence reviewed supports an account of institutional responsibilities and modernization priorities. It does not support a national ranking of training quality, a provincial comparison, or a claim that courses increase wages or employment. A fuller assessment would connect clearly defined courses with practical assessments, employer feedback, and follow-up evidence about graduates. Until such evidence is inspected, Iran’s industrial training should be understood through its documented institutions and projects, with outcomes left open for further research.

name: Management Skills
description: Management skills concern how organizations coordinate people, information, and resources. Documented Iranian examples include management education at the Industrial Management Institute and practical knowledge-management training involving public-sector institutions.

seo.title: Management Skills and Training in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand management education and practical organizational learning in Iran through documented institutions and training examples.

content.heading: A field spanning organizational functions
content.content:
Management skills are best understood as a collection of capabilities rather than a single qualification. Finance, staffing, marketing, and operational coordination involve different bodies of knowledge. The World Higher Education Database, maintained by the International Association of Universities, illustrates this breadth in its entry for Iran’s Industrial Management Institute, or IMI. Its listed fields include finance, human resources, industrial management, marketing, and transport management. [s1](https://whed.net/institutions/IAU-016832)

The database records IMI’s foundation in 1962 and identifies Tehran as its location. It also lists Master of Business Administration and Executive MBA programs, alongside other management-related provision. However, the entry states that it was updated in March 2019. It is therefore useful as evidence of an established management-education institution, while current admissions, course availability, and qualification arrangements require fresh confirmation. A directory listing cannot demonstrate the effectiveness of a course or a graduate’s workplace performance. [s1](https://whed.net/institutions/IAU-016832)

content.heading: Learning from organizational knowledge
content.content:
A practical example comes from a Tehran course held in August 2017 by the Asian Productivity Organization, or APO, with the National Iranian Productivity Organization and Iran’s Ministry of Energy. It addressed knowledge management: the organized use and sharing of what people and institutions know. The curriculum connected this subject with innovation, information technology, productivity, and service quality. [s2](https://www.apo-tokyo.org/aponews/apo-conducts-training-for-km-in-the-public-sector/)

The organizer’s account describes case studies, comparative country material, a visit to Niroo Research Institute, and individual action plans for applying learning within participants’ organizations. These activities show a training design that moved beyond presentations toward observation and planned application. They do not establish whether those plans were subsequently implemented or produced lasting improvements. The account is a report of a particular international course hosted in Iran, rather than a representative survey of Iranian managers. [s2](https://www.apo-tokyo.org/aponews/apo-conducts-training-for-km-in-the-public-sector/)

content.heading: Training institutions also need management capabilities
content.content:
Management development also appears within vocational education itself. UNESCO’s terms of reference for an instructor-training modernization project in Karaj include strengthening the capabilities of managers, researchers, and master trainers. The document connects institutional development with a revised approach to delivering training. This is evidence that the project treats organizational capability as part of educational improvement; it is not an evaluation showing that management performance improved. [s3](https://iran.un.org/en/download/184181/294666)

Together, these examples distinguish subject-based management education, focused professional courses, and organizational development inside a training institution. Their purposes overlap, but their results require different evidence. A program listing establishes subject coverage; a course report establishes documented activities; evidence of workplace change requires subsequent observation. This distinction is especially useful for international readers encountering unfamiliar qualification names or institutional claims. The available material introduces the field, while leaving national participation, regional access, and independently assessed effectiveness unresolved.

name: Entrepreneurship Education
description: Entrepreneurship education in Iran includes university learning and initiatives to develop entrepreneurs and their mentors. Research on students provides evidence about intentions and perceived capabilities, which must be distinguished from verified business creation or survival.

seo.title: Entrepreneurship Education in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iranian entrepreneurship education, university research, mentor training, and the distinction between intentions and business outcomes.

content.heading: Learning about enterprise and deciding to pursue it
content.content:
Entrepreneurship education involves learning associated with identifying opportunities and considering the creation or development of a venture. Iranian university research offers an important distinction: a student’s intention to become an entrepreneur is a different outcome from establishing an operating business. A study by Saeid Karimi and colleagues examined elective and compulsory entrepreneurship programs through questionnaires administered before and after participation. Its published abstract reports that elective programs increased entrepreneurial intention significantly, while the increase for compulsory programs was not statistically significant. [s1](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/jsbm.12137)

Both forms of provision showed positive changes in perceived behavioral control and subjective norms. In this research framework, these concern a person’s perceived ability to act and the social expectations surrounding that action. The distinction between elective and compulsory learning is educationally significant, but the abstract does not establish that choosing a course caused better outcomes. Nor does it report a national business-formation rate attributable to education. [s1](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/jsbm.12137)

content.heading: Students and educators may assess teaching differently
content.content:
Research on entrepreneurship programs in Iran’s applied-science and technology universities examined the perspectives of students and educators. Its abstract reports disagreement between the groups about relationships involving teaching methods and program impact. It also acknowledges that the selection of universities limits generalization. This supports a careful conclusion: evaluating provision requires attention to what learners experience, rather than relying exclusively on educators’ judgments. It does not justify labeling all Iranian entrepreneurship teaching effective or ineffective. [s2](https://www.emerald.com/et/article-abstract/61/7-8/781/72918/Evaluating-impact-of-entrepreneurship-education?redirectedFrom=fulltext)

The inspected material for these studies consists of published abstracts, so their detailed instruments, implementation conditions, and full statistical analyses are outside this account. Reported associations and changes should therefore remain attached to the specific studies. They should not be converted into claims about business survival, income, or jobs without follow-up evidence measuring those outcomes. [s1](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/jsbm.12137) [s2](https://www.emerald.com/et/article-abstract/61/7-8/781/72918/Evaluating-impact-of-entrepreneurship-education?redirectedFrom=fulltext)

content.heading: Developing the people who support entrepreneurs
content.content:
Entrepreneurship learning also extends beyond student courses. UNIDO documents an Iranian information and communication technology initiative combining startup-ecosystem analysis, training for entrepreneurs and mentors, and a proposed virtual entrepreneurship hub. Its page identifies the Erasmus Centre for Entrepreneurship as the provider for a series of trainer-development programs. This introduces another educational layer: improving the capabilities of people who coach or support entrepreneurs. [s3](https://www.unido.org/training-startup-coaches-in-Iran)

The page says applications for that edition are closed. It should consequently be read as documentation of an initiative, rather than as a current enrollment invitation. Its stated competitiveness objectives also require separate outcome evidence. [s3](https://www.unido.org/training-startup-coaches-in-Iran)

The central distinction is between providing entrepreneurship learning, changing participants’ attitudes or perceived capabilities, and producing durable enterprises. The inspected sources illuminate the first stages more clearly than the last. A fuller national account needs current curricula, evidence beyond selected university settings, and follow-up research tracing actual ventures over time.
